prompt: What makes an acid a strong acid?

choices.text: It dissociates 100% into ions in aqueous solution.

choices.why: Strength is about how completely an acid ionizes, not how much of it is dissolved. A dilute solution of HCl is still a strong acid.
Only 100% ionization makes an acid strong. An acid that is 99% ionized is still classified as weak.

choices.text: It contains more than one H atom.
choices.why: The number of H atoms doesn't decide strength. HCl has one H and is strong; H3PO4 has three and is weak.

explanation: Any acid that dissociates 100% into ions is called a strong acid. If it does not dissociate 100%, it is a weak acid.

prompt: An acid not listed among the strong acids is found to be 99% ionized in water. How is it classified?

choices.text: As a strong acid, because it is nearly completely ionized
choices.why: Strong means 100% ionized. Anything less, even 99%, is classified as weak.
Every acid is either strong (100% ionized) or weak (less than 100%).
Ionizing to release H^+ makes it an acid; the 99% makes it a weak one.

explanation: There are very few strong acids, and any acid not on that list is weak. It may be 1% ionized or 99% ionized, but it is still classified as a weak acid.

prompt: Which of these is a strong acid?

choices.why: Unlike HCl, HBr, and HI, hydrofluoric acid is not one of the strong acids, so it is weak.
Acetic acid is a weak acid, only about 5% ionized.
Phosphoric acid isn't on the list of strong acids, so it is weak.

explanation: The strong acids are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO3, and HClO4. HBr is on the list; HF, HC2H3O2, and H3PO4 are not, so they are weak.

prompt: Which of these acids is weak?

choices.why: HI is one of the strong acids, 100% ionized in water.
HNO3 is one of the strong acids.
HClO4 is one of the strong acids.

explanation: HF isn't on the short list of strong acids, so it is a weak acid, even though HCl, HBr, and HI are strong.

prompt: Which of these is a strong base?

choices.why: NH3 has no OH^− in its formula; it makes OH^− by reacting with water, and is a weak base.
CH3NH2 is like NH3, a base without OH^−, so it is weak.
This base contains no OH^− ions, so it can't be a strong base.

explanation: All strong bases are OH^− compounds, and there are very few of them: LiOH, NaOH, KOH, RbOH, CsOH, Mg(OH)2, Ca(OH)2, Sr(OH)2, and Ba(OH)2. KOH is on the list.

prompt: Why is NH3 a weak base?

choices.text: All strong bases are OH^− compounds, and NH3 has no OH^− in its formula; it depends on another mechanism.
NH3 is a gas, and gases can't be strong bases.
choices.why: Phase isn't the reason. NH3 is weak because it isn't an OH^− compound and isn't 100% ionized.
NH3 accepts protons from water. It is weak because it does so incompletely.

choices.text: NH3 is a strong base, not a weak one.
choices.why: NH3 is not on the short list of strong bases, all of which are OH^− compounds.

explanation: All strong bases are OH^− compounds. A base that depends on some other mechanism, such as NH3 reacting with water, will be a weak base.

prompt: Acetic acid, HC2H3O2, is only about 5% ionized in water. What is mostly present in a solution of acetic acid?

choices.why: That would be true only for a strong acid. With about 5% ionized, most of the acid stays as molecules.
Acetic acid is an acid; it releases some H^+, not OH^−.
Ionization makes H^+ and C2H3O2^−; no H2 gas forms.

explanation: Acetic acid is a weak acid, only about 5% ionized, so most of it remains as HC2H3O2 molecules. Its ionization is written as a reversible reaction: HC2H3O2 ⇌ H^+(aq) + C2H3O2^−(aq).

prompt: Why is the ionization of a weak acid written with a double arrow, ⇌?

choices.text: The reaction doesn't go 100% to completion, so it is written as a reversible reaction.

choices.why: The double arrow shows that the reaction runs in both directions and doesn't go to completion.

choices.text: Because weak acids produce two kinds of ions.
choices.why: Strong acids produce two kinds of ions too. The double arrow marks a reaction that doesn't go 100% to products.

choices.text: Because the reaction goes 100% to products.
choices.why: A reaction that goes 100% to products, like the ionization of a strong acid, is written with a single arrow.

explanation: Because the ionization of a weak acid does not go 100% to completion, it is more appropriate to write it as a reversible reaction, with a double arrow.

prompt: Which equation correctly shows the dissociation of Ba(OH)2 in water?

choices.text: Ba(OH)2 ⇌ Ba^2+(aq) + 2OH^−(aq), not going to completion
choices.why: Ba(OH)2 is a strong base, so it dissociates 100%: a single arrow.
Barium forms Ba^2+, and each formula unit releases two OH^− ions.
The OH^− ion stays together; Ba(OH)2 separates into Ba^2+ and OH^− ions.

explanation: Ba(OH)2 is an ionic compound of Ba^2+ and OH^− ions, and it is a strong base, so it separates completely: Ba(OH)2 → Ba^2+(aq) + 2OH^−(aq).

prompt: Which statement about the ionization HF → H^+(aq) + F^−(aq) is correct?

choices.text: It does not proceed 100% to products, because HF is a weak acid.
It proceeds 100% to products, because HF contains a halogen.
choices.why: HCl, HBr, and HI are strong, but HF is not on the strong acid list, so it is weak.

choices.text: It doesn't happen at all; HF is a base.
choices.why: HF releases H^+ in water, so it is an acid; it just doesn't ionize completely.
Acid ionization produces H^+ and the anion, here F^−.

explanation: HF is a weak acid, so its ionization does not proceed 100% to products and is better written HF ⇌ H^+(aq) + F^−(aq).

prompt: Which ions in a salt will hydrolyze and affect the acidity or basicity of the solution?

choices.text: Ions that are part of weak acids or weak bases
Ions that are part of strong acids or strong bases
choices.why: Those ions don't hydrolyze: any acid or base they would form is 100% ionized, so there is no net change.
Ions from strong acids and bases, like Na^+ and Cl^−, have no effect.

choices.text: No ions; salts are always neutral
choices.why: Salts like NaC2H3O2 and NH4Cl make basic and acidic solutions.

explanation: The general rule is that ions that are part of strong acids or bases will not hydrolyze, while ions that are part of weak acids or bases will hydrolyze.

prompt: What is a neutral salt?

choices.text: An ionic compound that does not affect the acidity or basicity of its aqueous solution
A salt with no electric charge
choices.why: All ionic compounds are neutral overall. A neutral salt is one whose solution is neither acidic nor basic.

choices.text: A salt that doesn't dissolve in water
choices.why: Neutral salts like NaCl dissolve well. Their ions simply don't change the acidity.

choices.text: Any salt made from a weak acid
choices.why: A salt of a weak acid's anion is usually basic, not neutral.

explanation: A neutral salt is any ionic compound that does not affect the acidity or basicity of its aqueous solution. NaCl is an example.

prompt: Why does NaCl form a neutral solution?

choices.text: Na^+ comes from the strong base NaOH and Cl^− from the strong acid HCl, so neither ion hydrolyzes with a net effect.

choices.why: NaCl dissolves readily, separating into Na^+ and Cl^− ions.

choices.text: Na^+ makes the solution acidic and Cl^− makes it basic, and they cancel.
choices.why: Neither ion changes the acidity at all, because each derives from a strong acid or base.

choices.text: NaCl reacts with water to form NaOH and HCl, which remain as molecules.
choices.why: NaOH and HCl are 100% ionized; any that formed would just remake water, leaving no net change.

explanation: If Na^+ hydrolyzed, it would make NaOH, a strong base that is 100% ionized; if Cl^− hydrolyzed, it would make HCl, a strong acid that is 100% ionized. Either way there is no net change, so NaCl is a neutral salt.

prompt: Why is a solution of sodium acetate, NaC2H3O2, slightly basic?

choices.text: The acetate ion takes H^+ from water to form the weak acid HC2H3O2, leaving OH^− ions behind.
The Na^+ ion takes OH^− from water.
choices.why: Na^+ comes from a strong base, so it has no effect. The acetate ion is what hydrolyzes.
NaC2H3O2 has no OH^−. It makes OH^− as acetate hydrolyzes.

choices.text: Acetate ions donate protons to water.
choices.why: That would make the solution acidic. Acetate accepts protons from water.

explanation: C2H3O2^− + H2O ⇌ HC2H3O2 + OH^−. Because HC2H3O2 is a weak acid, it forms whenever it can, and the OH^− ions produced make the solution basic: NaC2H3O2 is a basic salt.

prompt: Why is a solution of NH4Cl slightly acidic?

choices.text: NH4^+ comes from the weak base NH3, so it hydrolyzes: NH4^+ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O^+.
Cl^− comes from a weak acid and takes OH^− from water.
choices.why: Cl^− comes from HCl, a strong acid, so it doesn't hydrolyze.
OH^− would make the solution basic. NH4^+ produces H3O^+.

choices.text: Any salt containing nitrogen is acidic.
choices.why: It's the NH4^+ ion's link to the weak base NH3 that matters, not nitrogen in general.

explanation: The NH4^+ ion derives from the weak base NH3, so it hydrolyzes: NH4^+(aq) + H2O ⇌ NH3(aq) + H3O^+(aq). The H3O^+ makes the solution slightly acidic: NH4Cl is an acid salt.

prompt: A salt contains one ion from a strong acid or base and one ion from a weak acid. What kind of solution does it make?

choices.why: An ion from a weak acid takes H^+ from water and leaves OH^−, so the solution is basic.
The ion from the weak acid hydrolyzes, so the salt does affect the acidity.
The rule predicts it: an ion from a weak acid makes the solution basic.

explanation: Ions from strong acids or bases don't affect the acidity. An ion from a weak acid makes the solution basic; an ion from a weak base makes it acidic.

prompt: Is a solution of NaBr acidic, basic, or neutral?

choices.why: Br^− comes from HBr, a strong acid, so it doesn't hydrolyze.
Na^+ comes from NaOH, a strong base, so it doesn't hydrolyze.
Neither ion hydrolyzes at any concentration, so the solution is neutral.

explanation: Na^+ derives from the strong base NaOH and Br^− from the strong acid HBr, so neither ion affects the acidity: NaBr is a neutral salt.

prompt: Is a solution of NaF acidic, basic, or neutral?

choices.why: F^− comes from HF, a weak acid, so it hydrolyzes. Unlike NaCl, NaF is not neutral.
F^− takes H^+ from water to form HF, leaving OH^−, which makes the solution basic.
Na^+ has no effect, and F^− from a weak acid makes the solution basic.

explanation: Na^+ derives from a strong base and has no effect, but F^− derives from the weak acid HF: F^− + H2O ⇌ HF + OH^−. NaF is a basic salt.

prompt: Is a solution of NH4NO3 acidic, basic, or neutral?

choices.why: NH4^+ derives from a weak base, which makes the solution acidic, not basic.
NO3^− from the strong acid HNO3 has no effect, but NH4^+ from the weak base NH3 does.
NO3^− has no effect and NH4^+ makes the solution acidic.

explanation: NO3^− derives from the strong acid HNO3 and has no effect, while NH4^+ derives from the weak base NH3 and produces H3O^+: NH4NO3 is an acidic salt.

prompt: Is a solution of potassium acetate, KC2H3O2, acidic, basic, or neutral?

choices.why: It contains the anion of an acid, but that anion takes H^+ from water, leaving OH^−. The solution is basic.
K^+ has no effect, but C2H3O2^− from the weak acid HC2H3O2 hydrolyzes.
K^+ comes from a strong base, and acetate from a weak acid, so the solution is basic.

explanation: K^+ derives from the strong base KOH and has no effect; C2H3O2^− derives from the weak acid HC2H3O2 and makes OH^−. KC2H3O2 is a basic salt.

prompt: Is a solution of LiNO3 acidic, basic, or neutral?

choices.why: NO3^− comes from HNO3, a strong acid, so it doesn't hydrolyze.
Li^+ comes from LiOH, a strong base, so it doesn't hydrolyze.

choices.text: It depends on how much LiNO3 dissolves.
choices.why: Neither ion hydrolyzes, so the solution is neutral whatever the amount.

explanation: Li^+ derives from the strong base LiOH and NO3^− from the strong acid HNO3, so LiNO3 is a neutral salt.

prompt: Is a solution of Na3PO4 acidic, basic, or neutral?

choices.why: PO4^3− derives from H3PO4, which is not a strong acid, so it hydrolyzes.
The phosphate ion takes H^+ from water, leaving OH^−; that makes the solution basic.
Na^+ has no effect, and PO4^3−, from the weak acid H3PO4, makes the solution basic.

explanation: Na^+ derives from a strong base. PO4^3− derives from H3PO4, a weak acid, so it hydrolyzes and produces OH^−: Na3PO4 is a basic salt.

prompt: A student says NH4Cl makes a basic solution, because NH3 is a base. What is wrong?

choices.text: NH4^+ is the conjugate acid of NH3; an ion from a weak base makes the solution acidic.
Nothing is wrong; NH4Cl is basic.
choices.why: NH4^+ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O^+ produces hydronium ions, so the solution is acidic.

choices.text: NH4Cl is neutral, because it is a salt.
choices.why: Salts can be acidic, basic, or neutral. NH4^+ from a weak base makes this one acidic.

choices.text: NH4Cl is basic, but because of the Cl^−.
choices.why: Cl^− comes from the strong acid HCl and has no effect.

explanation: The NH4^+ ion derives from the weak base NH3, and it hydrolyzes to form NH3 and H3O^+. If an ion derives from a weak base, it makes the solution acidic.

prompt: The section says, "Any chance a weak acid has to form, it will." Which observation does this explain?

choices.text: Acetate ions take H^+ from water to form HC2H3O2, making sodium acetate solutions basic.
Cl^− ions take H^+ from water to form HCl.
choices.why: HCl is a strong acid, 100% ionized, so Cl^− has no net effect.
That is because HCl is a strong acid; the quote is about weak acids forming.
NaCl is neutral because its ions come from a strong acid and a strong base.

explanation: HC2H3O2 is a weak acid, so acetate ions combine with H^+ from water whenever they can, leaving OH^− and making the solution basic. A weak base forms when it can in the same way.

prompt: Ba(OH)2 is a strong base. What is [OH^−] in a 0.050 M Ba(OH)2 solution?
explanation: A strong base is 100% ionized, and each Ba(OH)2 releases two OH^− ions: [OH^−] = 2 × 0.050 M = 0.10 M.

prompt: HNO3 is a strong acid. What is [H^+] in a 0.025 M HNO3 solution?
explanation: A strong acid dissociates 100%, and each HNO3 releases one H^+: [H^+] = 0.025 M.

prompt: A 0.10 M solution of a weak acid HA is 2.0% ionized. What is [H^+]?
explanation: Only 2.0% of the acid ionizes: [H^+] = 0.020 × 0.10 M = 0.0020 M, far less than the 0.10 M a strong acid would give.
